analysis.one_liner: Kills a proposed rule that would raise what oil companies pay to drill on federal land.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 216-200 on March 20, 2024, almost entirely along party lines, but it never got a vote in the Senate and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would force the Bureau of Land Management to withdraw a proposed rule that rewrites how oil and gas leases are sold on public land, including carrying out changes Congress ordered in the Inflation Reduction Act, and would bar the agency from issuing any substantially similar rule. The House passed it 216-200, with only 3 Democrats joining 213 Republicans. The Senate never acted on it, and the bill died when the two-year Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies that lease federal land would keep paying the current lower royalty rate and would avoid the tighter lease terms in the proposed rule, which covers everything from how leases are offered for bidding to the financial assurances companies must post. Under the Inflation Reduction Act, the minimum royalty on new federal onshore leases rose to 16.67% from the old 12.5%; the proposed rule carries out that change and related process reforms, so blocking it protects drillers from the full cost shift.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil and gas companies on federal land

how_it_helps.text: Within 30 days of enactment, the BLM Director would have to withdraw the proposed rule 'Fluid Mineral Leases and Leasing Process' published in July 2023.
The agency would be barred from finalizing, implementing, or enforcing that rule or any substantially similar one, so the changes could not simply be reissued.

The rule the bill targets would change oil and gas leasing on public lands, including implementing provisions of the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 and the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act of 2021, which raised the minimum royalty companies pay and tightened the leasing process.
The bill was amended in committee and reported out on a 23-18 vote before reaching the floor.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, who would collect less from oil and gas taken from land they own, and people who use public lands and waters near drilling that would continue under the looser leasing terms. Treasury would forgo revenue from the higher royalty the Inflation Reduction Act set for new leases.

drawbacks.text: The bill would lock in the older, cheaper terms for drilling on federal land. The Inflation Reduction Act raised the minimum royalty on new onshore federal leases to 16.67% from 12.5%, and the rule the bill kills is part of putting that and related leasing changes into practice, so blocking it shifts value from the public treasury to leaseholders.

It is a blanket prohibition rather than a rewritten policy: the agency could not finalize the rule or anything substantially like it, so the specific problems the rule addressed, such as how leases are offered and what financial assurances drillers must post, would stay unresolved by legislation.

Supporters argued the rule would add cost and paperwork for producers and could discourage drilling on federal land, tightening supply. The CRS summary does not quantify that effect, so it rests on the industry-side argument rather than the record.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers little to ordinary people and carries a real cost: less money for the public from oil and gas taken from public land and continued leasing under looser terms. The industry-side argument, that the rule would discourage drilling and raise prices, is a plausible objection to the underlying rule, but the bill answers it by blocking the rule entirely rather than fixing any part of it, and it would also erase the royalty increase Congress itself wrote into law in 2022.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 216-200, but the Senate committee it was referred to the next day never took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Introduced in October 2023 by Rep. Lauren Boebert and referred to the House Natural Resources Committee, which ordered it reported on a 23-18 vote and reported it amended in February 2024.
The House considered it under a closed rule on March 20, 2024, meaning no floor amendments were allowed.
Rep. Katie Porter moved to send the bill back to committee with instructions; the motion failed 204-211, with all 204 voting Democrats in favor and all 211 voting Republicans against.
Final passage passed 216-200: 213 of 219 voting Republicans voted yes and 200 of 213 voting Democrats voted no, with 3 Democrats crossing over.

The Senate received the bill on March 21, 2024, and referred it to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, where it stayed with no further action until the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never became law, the proposed leasing changes were never blocked by Congress, so taxpayers and public-lands users kept the chance at the higher royalties and tighter terms the rule would have carried out. Had the bill passed, oil and gas companies holding federal leases would have come out ahead.

industries.industry: Oil and gas companies leasing federal land
industries.note: The bill would void a rule that raises the minimum royalty on new federal onshore leases to 16.67% under the Inflation Reduction Act and tightens how leases are sold, so drillers would keep the cheaper 12.5% royalty and looser terms. Their gain is directly a loss of revenue for the federal treasury, which holds the minerals in trust for the public.

industries.industry: Federal onshore drilling generally (including smaller operators)
industries.note: Blocking the rule also spares all federal-land producers the compliance costs of new bonding, bidding, and lease-sale requirements, which supporters argued protects production; smaller operators with thin margins benefit most from that relief.
